sources.title: INAH Mexico, Grandeza y Diversidad: Los Olmecas, primeros maestros
sources.note: Official synthesis covers flexible Preclassic chronology, San Jose Mogote, Monument 3, regional interaction, and the rise of Monte Alban.

sources.title: Smarthistory: Late Preclassic Mesoamerica, an introduction
sources.note: Scholarly overview distinguishes regions, farming communities, growing centers, visual traditions, and the long transition toward Mesoamerican cities.

sources.title: INAH: Monte Alban archaeological zone
sources.note: Official archaeological-zone account dates the city from about 500 BCE and describes the leveled hilltop, terraced slopes, monuments, tombs, agriculture, and Zapotec capital.

sources.title: INAH Places: Cuicuilco and early monumental architecture
sources.note: Official account describes Cuicuilco settlement, monumental construction, varied housing, farming, hydraulic works, exchange, and long occupation in the Basin of Mexico.

sources.title: INAH Cuicuilco Site Museum
sources.note: Official museum guide identifies evidence for everyday activities, tools, imported materials, ornament, figurines, ritual, health, and burial.

sources.title: INAH Arqueologia: Reinterpreting Cuicuilco
sources.note: Peer-reviewed INAH research reviews revised chronology, settlement layout, monumental construction, social differentiation, irrigation, and volcanic dating.

sources.title: INAH: A proposal for the pre-Hispanic history of Alpuyeca
sources.note: Official regional archaeology describes spring-side villages, rain-fed milpa cultivation, ceramics, and changing centers from 1500 BCE onward.

sources.title: Latin American Antiquity: Beginnings of Village Life in Eastern Mesoamerica
sources.note: Peer-reviewed excavations document northern Honduran settlement before 1600 BCE, sophisticated pottery, and wide exchange by 1100 to 900 BCE.

sources.title: Latin American Antiquity: Archaic Origins of the Lowland Maya
sources.note: Peer-reviewed review separates subsistence, technology, settlement, and radiocarbon evidence while keeping pottery before 1000 BCE uncertain.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: Gathering and Sowing across the Central Maya Lowlands
sources.note: Peer-reviewed archaeobotanical review documents wild foods, maize, manioc, chili peppers, village life, canals, terraces, and uneven preservation.

sources.title: Antiquity: Preclassic Maya caches in residential contexts at Ceibal
sources.note: Peer-reviewed household archaeology distinguishes domestic floor and construction deposits from public plaza rituals between 1000 and 350 BCE.

sources.title: Latin American Antiquity: Preclassic and Classic Maya obsidian at Ceibal
sources.note: Peer-reviewed sourcing identifies changing Guatemalan obsidian suppliers and the economic importance of highland-lowland exchange across Preclassic phases.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: Middle Preclassic pottery production in northern Maya lowlands
sources.note: Peer-reviewed chemical study finds local pottery production from 900 BCE onward and cautions against simplistic style-based chronology.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: Altica, Coapexco, and Formative obsidian exchange
sources.note: Peer-reviewed geochemical research reconstructs household exchange, gateway communities, flake tools, processing, and distribution in the Basin of Mexico.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: Formative obsidian blade trade
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study distinguishes traded prismatic blades from the later extensive movement of prepared blade cores.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: Middle Preclassic landscape investment
sources.note: Peer-reviewed excavations document reservoirs, catchments, terraces, dry-season storage, collaborative labor, and dating after about 800 BCE.

sources.title: UNESCO: Tehuacan-Cuicatlan water-management comparison
sources.note: Official dossier compares dated canals, dams, reservoirs, wells, terraces, aqueducts, and regional functions without making them uniform.

sources.title: American Antiquity: A Preclassic Maya Water System
sources.note: Peer-reviewed report documents drainage, canals, raised platforms, quarrying, and watershed modification at Cerros from 300 BCE onward.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: Ancestral Maya domesticated waterscapes
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis describes canals, shallow lakes, gardens, fish, turtles, mollusks, waterfowl, and ecological water management at Preclassic sites.

sources.title: Smarthistory: Tlatilco figurines
sources.note: Scholarly museum essay describes a lakeside farming village, maize, fish, birds, houses, burials, figurines, hairstyles, and interpretive limits.

sources.title: Princeton University Art Museum: Art of the Ancient Americas
sources.note: University museum catalogue securely dates specific Tlatilco figurines to 1400 through 1100 BCE and records their material and provenance.

sources.title: PubMed: Health and agricultural intensification in prehistoric Oaxaca
sources.note: Peer-reviewed skeletal study compares 1400 to 500 BCE nonintensive agriculture with later intensification and finds no simple health decline.

sources.title: PLOS One: Sulfur isotopes in the Eastern Maya lowlands
sources.note: Peer-reviewed isotope study documents maize-rich but locally varied diets and explains limits involving age, sex, ecology, mobility, and protein sources.

sources.title: American Antiquity: Agricultural demographic transition in Mesoamerica
sources.note: Peer-reviewed regional study links changing maize forms and standardized grinding equipment to long uneven demographic transitions.

sources.title: Cambridge: Ancient Oaxaca, regional setting for an early state
sources.note: University-press synthesis covers households, public buildings, conflict, Monument 3, calendar interpretation, and Monte Alban state formation.

sources.title: PNAS: The origin of war, new dates from ancient Mexico
sources.note: Peer-reviewed radiocarbon study dates burned Oaxacan structures and examines conflict, households, Monument 3, and San Jose Mogote chronology.

sources.title: FAMSI: Zapotec Writing, Formative narratives
sources.note: Specialist epigraphic figures show proposed readings and dates while exposing uncertainty around early Oaxacan glyphs and calendrical names.

sources.title: Science: Olmec Origins of Mesoamerican Writing
sources.note: Peer-reviewed report dates San Andres symbols near 650 BCE and attributes them to a specific Olmec political context by La Venta.

sources.title: Science Advances: An early Maya calendar record from San Bartolo
sources.note: Peer-reviewed stratigraphy and radiocarbon dates place a 7 Deer day sign between 300 and 200 BCE, inside the atlas gap.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Olmec Art
sources.note: Museum scholarship describes San Lorenzo, portable styles, wooden and stone sculpture, ceramics, exchange, and regional imitation after maize agriculture spread.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: Early Olmec carved pottery
sources.note: Peer-reviewed compositional and stylistic research separates exported Gulf vessels from numerous locally made adaptations in distant regions.

sources.title: PNAS: Chemical and archaeological evidence for early cacao beverages
sources.note: Peer-reviewed residue chemistry documents cacao drinks at Puerto Escondido by 1100 BCE and regional vessel connections without supplying recipes.

sources.title: Cambridge: Teotihuacan in a Wider Perspective
sources.note: University-press synthesis dates rapid Teotihuacan growth from about 100 BCE and preserves uncertainty about institutions and population estimates.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: Formative subsistence at Altica
sources.note: Peer-reviewed macro- and microbotanical evidence documents a maize-growing rural community and changing plant use in the northern Basin.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: Reframing Formative Altica
sources.note: Peer-reviewed project identifies Altica as the earliest known settled village in the Teotihuacan Valley and stresses preservation limits.

sources.title: Ancient Mesoamerica: The Ceramics of Cuello, Belize
sources.note: Peer-reviewed reanalysis establishes a long local ceramic sequence from about 1200 BCE and demonstrates changing regional ceramic spheres.
